title: Trump Admin Violated Court Orders in at Least 31 Lawsuits in 15 Months
description_short: Trump Admin Violated Court Orders in at Least 31 Lawsuits in 15 Months
description_medium: An Associated Press investigation published May 2, 2026, documented that in the first 15 months of Trump's second term, district court judges found the administration in violation of court orders in at least 31 separate lawsuits — covering mass layoffs, deportations, immigration practices, and spending cuts. In one case, Judge Sunshine Sykes accused Trump officials of seeking to 'erode any semblance of separation of powers,' saying the conduct was only possible 'in a world where the Constitution does not exist.'

The supplied account says the cases concerned mass layoffs, deportations, immigration practices and spending reductions. One example involved Judge Sunshine Sykes criticizing officials' conduct as threatening the separation of powers. title: U.S. Citizen Dulce Diaz Morales Held 25 Days After ICE Rejected Her Maryland Birth Certificate
description_short: U.S. Citizen Dulce Diaz Morales Held 25 Days After ICE Rejected Her Maryland Birth Certificate
description_medium: In late 2025, 22-year-old Dulce Consuelo Diaz Morales was arrested by ICE agents despite her attorneys providing her Maryland birth certificate proving she was born in the United States. DHS contested her citizenship claim, alleging she entered the country illegally, and held her in an immigrant detention facility for 25 days before finally releasing her. Her case was cited by ProPublica in April 2026 alongside the Brian Morales deportation as evidence that ICE agents are systematically ignoring documentary proof of citizenship.
description_long: ICE arrested 22-year-old Dulce Consuelo Diaz Morales in late 2025 despite her lawyers presenting a Maryland birth certificate to support her U.S. citizenship, according to the supplied account. DHS disputed that claim and alleged that she entered the country illegally. She remained in immigration detention for 25 days before being released. The opposing accounts make attribution important: the lawyers' documentary argument and the department's allegation should both appear without treating the department's assertion as a final finding. ProPublica cited her case in April 2026 alongside the Brian Morales deportation when examining immigration officers' treatment of citizenship evidence. title: Senate Holds 'Rogue Judges' Impeachment Hearing Targeting Boasberg and Boardman
description_short: Senate Holds 'Rogue Judges' Impeachment Hearing Targeting Boasberg and Boardman
description_medium: On January 7, 2026, the Senate Judiciary subcommittee chaired by Ted Cruz held a hearing titled 'Impeachment: Holding Rogue Judges Accountable,' pushing to remove U.S. District Judges James Boasberg and Deborah Boardman for rulings against the Trump administration. Cruz sent a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson demanding the House advance impeachment proceedings. Georgetown law professor Stephen Vladeck testified that in U.S. history no judge had ever been impeached purely for the substance of their rulings, calling the move constitutionally unprecedented.
description_long: A Senate Judiciary subcommittee chaired by Ted Cruz held a January 7, 2026 hearing on using impeachment against judges. The supplied account describes an effort directed at District Judges James Boasberg and Deborah Boardman following rulings against the administration. Cruz also wrote House Speaker Mike Johnson asking the House to advance impeachment proceedings. Georgetown law professor Stephen Vladeck testified that no judge in U.S. history had been impeached solely for the substance of judicial rulings. His assessment explains the constitutional concern raised by treating disagreement with decisions as grounds for removal. The hearing and letter were political and oversight actions; they did not themselves remove either judge or establish that impeachment offenses had been proved. The supported event records the initiative and the expert testimony opposing its premise. It does not establish that the House subsequently adopted articles, that the Senate convicted a judge, or that every participant agreed on the legal standard.

title: ICE Arrests Emmy Award Journalist Mario Guevara While Reporting Deports After 112 Days
description_short: ICE Arrests Emmy Award Journalist Mario Guevara While Reporting Deports After 112 Days
description_medium: On June 14, 2025, Emmy Award-winning Salvadoran journalist Mario Guevara, who held a valid US work permit and press credentials, was arrested by Atlanta-area police while livestreaming an anti-Trump protest and transferred to ICE detention. Despite all criminal charges being dismissed by local prosecutors, Guevara was held for 112 days across six detention facilities, placed in solitary confinement, and deported to El Salvador on October 3, 2025. His lawyers argued the detention was in retaliation for his critical coverage of ICE operations.
description_long: Journalist Mario Guevara was arrested by police in the Atlanta area on June 14, 2025 while livestreaming an anti-Trump protest, according to the supplied account. He held press credentials and a valid U.S. work permit. After the arrest, he was transferred into ICE detention. Local prosecutors dismissed the criminal charges, but he remained detained for 112 days across six facilities, including time in solitary confinement, before deportation to El Salvador on October 3. His lawyers argued that the detention was retaliation for his critical reporting on ICE. That explanation should remain attributed to counsel rather than presented as an adjudicated motive. The chronology shows that dismissal of the local charges did not end his immigration detention, making the distinction between criminal and immigration proceedings central to the case. The event records the arrest, extended custody and removal. It does not supply a final legal ruling confirming the alleged retaliatory purpose.

title: US Citizen Leo Garcia Venegas Detained by ICE Three Times in One Year
description_short: US Citizen Leo Garcia Venegas Detained by ICE Three Times in One Year
description_medium: Leonardo Garcia Venegas, a US citizen of Mexican descent in Alabama, was detained by immigration agents three separate times — in 2025 and again on May 2, 2026 — despite presenting a valid Alabama REAL ID each time. Agents dismissed the REAL ID as fake, tackled and shackled him. ICE officials at a border security conference the same week falsely stated citizens had been detained 'zero times' by mistake. Venegas filed a federal lawsuit; the government argued the sweeps were constitutionally valid.
description_long: The supplied account describes three immigration-enforcement detentions of Leonardo Garcia Venegas, a U.S. citizen of Mexican descent living in Alabama, during 2025 and again on May 2, 2026. It says he presented an Alabama REAL ID each time, that agents dismissed it as fake, and that he was tackled and shackled. Venegas filed a federal lawsuit challenging the actions. The government defended the sweeps as constitutionally valid. The account also contrasts his experience with ICE officials' statement at a border-security conference that citizens had been mistakenly detained zero times. The lawsuit and the official statement therefore provide competing material for scrutiny of how agents recognized citizenship during enforcement operations. A filed suit is not a final damages judgment, and the government's defense is not a court ruling that every detention was lawful.
